passage: At the Andheri office, Nilesh wore his short nights like a medal. "Sleep is for after the promotion," he joked by the coffee machine, refilling his mug yet again. In the client review he cut Lalit off twice and snapped, "Can we move faster?" Then Lalit pointed at the screen: the totals in Nilesh's sheet were off by a whole column. The room went quiet. Back at his desk, Nilesh's hands were jittery. He scrolled back through the week: a wrong date in an email, a missed call, a sharp reply to the intern. All since the late nights began. That evening he shut his laptop early and left it in the office drawer.

qa.q: What was wrong with Nilesh's sheet?
qa.a: The totals were off by a whole column.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling back at his desk?
qa.a: He felt shaken and embarrassed, with jittery hands, as he saw his slips had piled up since the late nights began.

qa.q: What could Nilesh keep doing, and why?
qa.a: Protecting his sleep, as he started to by leaving the laptop at the office, since rest would sharpen the judgment his late nights were wearing down.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when Nilesh cut in twice?
qa.a: Lalit was likely irritated at being cut off, yet still pointed out the error that mattered.

grounding: Shows a young professional treating short sleep as dedication, then seeing poorer judgment, irritability and leaning on coffee lower his work.

passage:
Subject: A confession, and a question

Dear Arnab,
You once told our class that the best architects protect their mornings. I laughed. In my first year at the firm I slept as little as I could and called it commitment. I answered client mail after midnight and was proud of my red eyes.
Lately it has gone wrong. Last week I approved a drawing with a staircase that went nowhere. In meetings I bite people's heads off, then spend the evening apologising. I lean on coffee all day and still feel foggy. The hours were meant to make me better at this, and they are making me worse.
I have started small: phone off at night, a proper breakfast, no email in bed. Did you ever go through this? How did you learn to leave work at a sane hour without feeling lazy?
Warmly,
Zeenat

qa.q: What was wrong with the drawing Zeenat approved?
qa.a: It had a staircase that went nowhere.

qa.q: How does Zeenat feel about the long hours now?
qa.a: Zeenat feels worried and let down, realising the hours meant to prove commitment are making the work worse.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's first steps seem sensible, and what else could help?
qa.a: Phone off at night, a proper breakfast and no email in bed are good starts; talking with a manager about workload could help too.

qa.q: How might Arnab react to this email?
qa.a: Arnab might feel concerned but not surprised, having once warned about protecting mornings, and glad to be asked.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who treated little sleep as commitment now noticing mistakes, irritability in meetings and reliance on coffee.

passage:
Wednesday, 11:50 pm, still at the desk
Fifth night this week under five hours. I used to be proud of that. The team calls me the machine.
Today the machine sent the client the wrong spreadsheet, the one full of our internal comments. Suraj caught it before they opened it, thank God. Then in the 4 pm meeting I snapped at Suraj when he asked a simple question, and the whole room went quiet. My fourth coffee of the day was in my hand.
On the metro home I did the maths. Longest hours in the team, most mistakes this month. The hours aren't making me better. They're making me slower and meaner.
Tomorrow: laptop shut at ten, no coffee after two, and I apologise to Suraj first thing.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What did Gurpreet send the client by mistake?
qa.a: The wrong spreadsheet, the one full of internal comments.

qa.q: How is Gurpreet feeling on the metro home?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels uneasy and a little ashamed, seeing that the long hours are making the work slower and the temper meaner.

qa.q: Which step in Gurpreet's plan matters most, and why?
qa.a: Shutting the laptop at ten, because protecting sleep tackles the cause of the mistakes and irritability; the apology then repairs the damage.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Gurpreet snapped in the meeting?
qa.a: Suraj was probably hurt and embarrassed in front of the team, especially after quietly catching Gurpreet's mistake.

grounding: Shows a young professional who treated short sleep as dedication noticing mistakes, irritability in meetings and leaning on coffee.

passage: At the sugar mill outside Baramati, Parveen had become famous for never going home. She took the night crushing shift, stayed on for the morning meeting, and drank the canteen's strong tea by the steel tumbler. "Real dedication," the manager said. But on Tuesday she signed off a maintenance sheet without checking the second page, and a belt she had marked safe snapped an hour later. Nobody was hurt, but the line stopped for three hours. In the meeting she snapped at Chaitanya when he asked about it, then went hot with shame. Chaitanya found her by the cane yard afterwards. "You've been here thirty hours, Parveen." She stared at the heaps of cane. The hours were supposed to make her better. That evening she asked the manager to keep her to one shift, went home, and slept till the next afternoon.

qa.q: What happened an hour after Parveen signed the maintenance sheet?
qa.a: A belt she had marked safe snapped.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling after snapping at Chaitanya?
qa.a: She went hot with shame, embarrassed and shaken by both her mistake and her temper.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that addressed the real problem?
qa.a: She asked the manager to keep her to one shift and went home to sleep, treating rest as part of doing the job well.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Parveen's long hours?
qa.a: He sees them as the cause of her mistake rather than proof of dedication, and says so gently by pointing out the thirty hours.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose long hours on little sleep lead to a costly misjudgment and irritability, lowering the performance they were meant to raise.

passage: Gabriel, two years into a consulting job in Sao Paulo, liked boasting about how little he slept. He answered emails at one in the morning and was at his desk by seven, proud of it. By June his coffee count had doubled. In a client meeting he snapped at Wei, his teammate, over a small slide error, then made a bigger one himself: he quoted last year's figures. Afterwards Wei found him staring at the lift doors. 'You're working longer and getting worse,' Wei said quietly. 'That's not dedication, that's debt.' The words stung, but Gabriel checked his own error log. It was true. He began shutting his laptop at eleven.

qa.q: What mistake did Gabriel make in the client meeting?
qa.a: He quoted last year's figures.

qa.q: How did Gabriel feel when Wei called it debt?
qa.a: He felt stung, but when he checked his own error log he saw it was true.

qa.q: What did Gabriel change?
qa.a: He began shutting his laptop at eleven to protect his sleep.

qa.q: What is it like for Wei to be snapped at over a small slide error?
qa.a: Wei probably felt hurt and unfairly treated, yet chose to speak honestly and kindly afterwards.

grounding: A young professional treats short sleep as dedication until irritability and errors show it is lowering his performance.
